[[:db/retract 17592186184779 :question/answer-fields 17592186183283] {:db/id 17592186184175 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d0d68cfe-73a4-5cae-a88d-ce4c5ac5ed06" "question-c0bd3b27-d4c9-5213-b407-098030561a8e"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186184074 :question/problem "Find the distance between the vector $\mathbf{x}$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors $\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \},$ where
![](images/51/5154eac29b8dee2a4f1ae4212306f80d5ff7975d38751a222ef2027d35acc234.svg)" :question/worked-solution "The orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T\,\mathbf{x}.
$$

In our case, we have 
![](images/ac/acee6cac9fd5dec811783141ecdcfd07402d6482146cdbdcac8f6e536416f0b7.svg)

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}]\,\cdot \,[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\,\,\,\,\cdot \,[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 5 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}4 & 8 \\ 8 & 18\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ 16\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}9 & -4 \\ -4 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ 16\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-7 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 5 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=\overset{^}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the distance between $\mathbf{x}$ and the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}d(x,\overset{^}{x}) & =‖x-\overset{^}{x}‖ \\  & =\sqrt{({x}_{1}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{1})^{2}+({x}_{2}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{2})^{2}+({x}_{3}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{3})^{2}+({x}_{4}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{4})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3-(-3))^{2}+(5-5)^{2}+(-1-1)^{2}+(3-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{0+0+4+4} \\  & =\sqrt{8} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186184111 :question/problem "Find the acute angle between the vector $\mathbf{x}$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors $\{ \mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2\},$ where
![](images/13/13b2b59a69e2fd1562f9b835128a16332c7fbd32646f662efe7dbf06bf5cac56.svg)" :question/worked-solution "The orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T\,\mathbf{x}.
$$

In our case, we have
![](images/bb/bb65806cb07e71dc92a5c55c210df1112da1f2500ed6cf18ef2a373d155aea94.svg)
Therefore, we get the following projection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ -3 & -3 \\ -3 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}3 & -3 & -3 \\ 3 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ -3 & -3 \\ -3 & 3\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & -3 & -3 \\ 3 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ -3 & -3 \\ -3 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}27 & 9 \\ 9 & 27\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ -3 & -3 \\ -3 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{72}[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ -3 & -3 \\ -3 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The acute angle between $\mathbf{x}$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $\mathbf{x}$ and $\textrm{proj}_S \mathbf{x}.$ Equivalently, it is the acute angle between $\mathbf{x}$ and any non-zero vector that is parallel to $\textrm{proj}_S \mathbf{x}.$ So, to make calculations easier, we can find the angle between the vectors

![](images/54/54a3c6bd24d0c021c0aa65ca1f12c6470b83744c46f984bdb076287b076fc9c1.svg)

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{0\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 1+0\cdot 0}{\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}\sqrt{{(-1)}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1}\cdot \sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\theta = \arccos\left( \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}2\right)= \dfrac\pi 4,
$$

which is already an acute angle, as desired." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186184075 :question/problem "Given the vector $\mathbf{x}$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the solution space of the system.
![](images/5a/5ad675762a16e4c81d5d83161dc24646121e4ca10b1e8a4957d7e9a317fc1fc4.svg)" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 & 0 \\ 2 & -4 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2,$ and $x_3$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get $x_1 = 2x_2-3x_3.$ Therefore, the general solution is

Consequently, 

![](images/93/9335bf579d464c3e54a92459199d585c8e42b5ef21ee9382436439d050338c9e.svg)
is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we let $A$ be a matrix whose columns equal the elements of $\mathcal B,$ and we find the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the solution space of the system as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2 \\ 14\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}5 & -6 \\ -6 & 10\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}10 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{14}[\begin{aligned}10 & 6 \\ 6 & 5\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}10 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 8 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-d0d68cfe-73a4-5cae-a88d-ce4c5ac5ed06" :question/id #uuid "d0d68cfe-73a4-5cae-a88d-ce4c5ac5ed06" :question/math-academy-id "q-139469" :question/problem "Find the distance between the vector $x$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -3 \\ -3\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/worked-solution "The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ -2 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ -2 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\,\cdot \,[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ -2 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\,\,\,\,\cdot \,[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -3 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ -2 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}9 & 0 \\ 0 & 10\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ -2 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{90}[\begin{aligned}10 & 0 \\ 0 & 9\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ -2 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=\overset{^}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the distance between $x$ and the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}d(x,\overset{^}{x}) & =‖x-\overset{^}{x}‖ \\  & =\sqrt{({x}_{1}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{1})^{2}+({x}_{2}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{2})^{2}+({x}_{3}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{3})^{2}+({x}_{4}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{4})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(1-2)^{2}+(2-2)^{2}+(-3-(-1))^{2}+(-3-0)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+0+4+9} \\  & =\sqrt{14}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-db7e3155-6118-5747-b4e5-472254e85f83"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-db7e3155-6118-5747-b4e5-472254e85f83" :answer-field/id #uuid "db7e3155-6118-5747-b4e5-472254e85f83" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-db2fadc7-9954-5d2d-9567-580bac75c277" :answer-field/choices ["answer-c6a4b7c1-b28b-59e9-b2e0-44d2e77e5df9" "answer-6042ceb6-39dd-5861-ab98-2ba38c0dfad7" "answer-ff56f552-cb5d-52ad-a5a1-61418ef3f448" "answer-db2fadc7-9954-5d2d-9567-580bac75c277" "answer-6b6a5f2f-76cf-57a5-b55b-09e192c66fac"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c6a4b7c1-b28b-59e9-b2e0-44d2e77e5df9" :answer/id #uuid "c6a4b7c1-b28b-59e9-b2e0-44d2e77e5df9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2\sqrt{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6042ceb6-39dd-5861-ab98-2ba38c0dfad7" :answer/id #uuid "6042ceb6-39dd-5861-ab98-2ba38c0dfad7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ff56f552-cb5d-52ad-a5a1-61418ef3f448" :answer/id #uuid "ff56f552-cb5d-52ad-a5a1-61418ef3f448" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{11}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-db2fadc7-9954-5d2d-9567-580bac75c277" :answer/id #uuid "db2fadc7-9954-5d2d-9567-580bac75c277" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{14}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6b6a5f2f-76cf-57a5-b55b-09e192c66fac" :answer/id #uuid "6b6a5f2f-76cf-57a5-b55b-09e192c66fac" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{15}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-c0bd3b27-d4c9-5213-b407-098030561a8e" :question/id #uuid "c0bd3b27-d4c9-5213-b407-098030561a8e" :question/math-academy-id "q-139473" :question/problem "Find the distance between the vector $x$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 6 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/worked-solution "The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 2 \\ -2 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 2 \\ -2 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 2 \\ -2 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 6 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}8 & -4 \\ -4 & 6\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{16}[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=\overset{^}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, the distance between $x$ and the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}d(x,\overset{^}{x}) & =‖x-\overset{^}{x}‖ \\  & =\sqrt{({x}_{1}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{1})^{2}+({x}_{2}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{2})^{2}+({x}_{3}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{3})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(3-3)^{2}+(6-1)^{2}+(4-(-1))^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25+25} \\  & =\sqrt{50} \\  & =5\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ba894365-a618-5f73-93d7-cf99f582f802"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-ba894365-a618-5f73-93d7-cf99f582f802" :answer-field/id #uuid "ba894365-a618-5f73-93d7-cf99f582f802" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-1a899cfc-2b1e-5341-b7ff-75e82ccc677e" :answer-field/choices ["answer-eef9c29f-2ba3-5765-9533-90dd311f676f" "answer-0f092c3d-8556-5f6a-af54-6cf54502714d" "answer-facc80f1-1b35-55ea-977b-cfdffdd16d9d" "answer-1a899cfc-2b1e-5341-b7ff-75e82ccc677e" "answer-ee402ce0-013b-55b8-989b-cc8ea6267cb7"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-eef9c29f-2ba3-5765-9533-90dd311f676f" :answer/id #uuid "eef9c29f-2ba3-5765-9533-90dd311f676f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2\sqrt{13}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0f092c3d-8556-5f6a-af54-6cf54502714d" :answer/id #uuid "0f092c3d-8556-5f6a-af54-6cf54502714d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3\sqrt{6}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-facc80f1-1b35-55ea-977b-cfdffdd16d9d" :answer/id #uuid "facc80f1-1b35-55ea-977b-cfdffdd16d9d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4\sqrt{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1a899cfc-2b1e-5341-b7ff-75e82ccc677e" :answer/id #uuid "1a899cfc-2b1e-5341-b7ff-75e82ccc677e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5\sqrt{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ee402ce0-013b-55b8-989b-cc8ea6267cb7" :answer/id #uuid "ee402ce0-013b-55b8-989b-cc8ea6267cb7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "7" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186185333 :tutorial/content "One use for finding the orthogonal projection of a vector onto a subspace is to find the shortest distance between the vector and the subspace.

Given a vector $\mathbf{x}$ and a subspace $S = \textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \},$ the **distance between $\mathbf{x}$ and $S$** is given by 

$$
\Vert \mathbf{x} - \textrm{proj}_{S}\mathbf{x} \Vert
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/d1/d10fd1778529183deb6912cebe9d2b7ad405091fe21a261c464d3d22c6d0860b.png)

Let's find the distance between the vector $\mathbf{x}$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors $\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2 \},$ where

![](images/83/83f52159171e736c7ee9edbd0593442d2282572db667eca483e5a77d0b73c9f7.svg)

The orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T\,\mathbf{x}.
$$

In this case, we have 
![](images/9e/9eca38b4b340e44108b073e3f939ce29ae96345b9c1870b9e2cc57a98f9cb077.svg)
Therefore, we get the following projection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 4 & 9\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}9 & -4 \\ -4 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=\overset{^}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, using the distance formula, the distance between $\mathbf{x}$ and the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}d(x,\overset{^}{x}) & =‖x-\overset{^}{x}‖ \\  & =\sqrt{({x}_{1}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{1})^{2}+({x}_{2}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{2})^{2}+({x}_{3}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{3})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(0-(-2))^{2}+(2-2)^{2}+(4-2)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+0+4} \\  & =\sqrt{8} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** Recall that the vector $\textbf{x}-\textrm{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x},$ whose norm $\| \textbf{x}-\textrm{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x} \|$ represents the distance from $\mathbf{x}$ to $S,$ is sometimes called the **vector rejection of $\mathbf{x}$ from $S.$**" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186185334 :tutorial/content "As well as finding the distance between a vector and a subspace, we can also use the vector's orthogonal projection onto the subspace to find the angle between the vector and the subspace.

Given a vector $\mathbf{x}$ and a subspace $S = \textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \},$ the **acute angle between $\mathbf{x}$ and $S$** is the acute angle formed by $\mathbf{x}$ and its orthogonal projection $\textrm{proj}_S \mathbf{x},$ as shown below:

![](images/1c/1c9fd00ab46691fefc65ffa6478ed589fbad1df6bfd19b913c6a4a94ae0358a0.png)

Let's return to our previous example, where we had

![](images/3c/3c881ed55614722cf3cfe5c969c8c05a0c093e87cf1d2aa1221dbfc741455b92.svg)

Previously, we found that the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ into the subspace spanned by $\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}$ is

![](images/6a/6a060f96f72ece67567be5d0deb70042fa50ba2f005a1539c67383f6de3e1426.svg)

We can compute the cosine of the angle between $\mathbf x$ and $\textrm{proj}_S \mathbf x$ using the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x\cdot {\text{proj}}_{S}x}{||x||\cdot ||{\text{proj}}_{S}x||} \\  & =\frac{0\cdot (-2)+2\cdot 2+4\cdot 2}{\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{4}^{2}}\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{12}{\sqrt{20}\sqrt{12}} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 2\cdot 3}{2\sqrt{5}\cdot 2\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\theta = \arccos\left(  \dfrac{\sqrt3}{\sqrt5}\right) \approx 39.23^{\circ},
$$

which is already an acute angle." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186184403 :activity/expected-seconds 1260.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

Given a vector $\mathbf{x}$ and a subspace $S = \textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \},$ the **distance between $\mathbf{x}$ and $S$** is given by 

$$
\Vert \mathbf{x} - \textrm{proj}_{S}\mathbf{x} \Vert
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/d1/d10fd1778529183deb6912cebe9d2b7ad405091fe21a261c464d3d22c6d0860b.png)

Let's find the distance between the vector $\mathbf{x}$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors $\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2 \},$ where

![](images/83/83f52159171e736c7ee9edbd0593442d2282572db667eca483e5a77d0b73c9f7.svg)

The orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T\,\mathbf{x}.
$$

In this case, we have 
![](images/9e/9eca38b4b340e44108b073e3f939ce29ae96345b9c1870b9e2cc57a98f9cb077.svg)
Therefore, we get the following projection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 4 & 9\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}9 & -4 \\ -4 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=\overset{^}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, using the distance formula, the distance between $\mathbf{x}$ and the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}d(x,\overset{^}{x}) & =‖x-\overset{^}{x}‖ \\  & =\sqrt{({x}_{1}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{1})^{2}+({x}_{2}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{2})^{2}+({x}_{3}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{3})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(0-(-2))^{2}+(2-2)^{2}+(4-2)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+0+4} \\  & =\sqrt{8} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** Recall that the vector $\textbf{x}-\textrm{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x},$ whose norm $\| \textbf{x}-\textrm{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x} \|$ represents the distance from $\mathbf{x}$ to $S,$ is sometimes called the **vector rejection of $\mathbf{x}$ from $S.$**" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186185334 :tutorial/content "As well as finding the distance between a vector and a subspace, we can also use the vector's orthogonal projection onto the subspace to find the angle between the vector and the subspace.

Given a vector $\mathbf{x}$ and a subspace $S = \textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \},$ the **distance between $\mathbf{x}$ and $S$** is given by 

$$
\Vert \mathbf{x} - \textrm{proj}_{S}\mathbf{x} \Vert
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/d1/d10fd1778529183deb6912cebe9d2b7ad405091fe21a261c464d3d22c6d0860b.png)

![](images/83/83f52159171e736c7ee9edbd0593442d2282572db667eca483e5a77d0b73c9f7.svg)

The orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T\,\mathbf{x}.
$$

![](images/9e/9eca38b4b340e44108b073e3f939ce29ae96345b9c1870b9e2cc57a98f9cb077.svg)
Therefore, we get the following projection: 

$$

$$

 

Finally, using the distance formula, the distance between $\mathbf{x}$ and the subspace $S$ is given by

$$

$$

{:db/id 17592186184985 :step/content {:db/id 17592186185333 :tutorial/content "One use for finding the orthogonal projection of a vector onto a subspace is to find the shortest distance between the vector and the subspace.

Given a vector $\mathbf{x}$ and a subspace $S = \textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \},$ the **distance between $\mathbf{x}$ and $S$** is given by 

$$
\Vert \mathbf{x} - \textrm{proj}_{S}\mathbf{x} \Vert
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/d1/d10fd1778529183deb6912cebe9d2b7ad405091fe21a261c464d3d22c6d0860b.png)

Let's find the distance between the vector $\mathbf{x}$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors $\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2 \},$ where

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$

The orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T\,\mathbf{x}.
$$

In this case, we have 

$$
[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 4 & 9\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}9 & -4 \\ -4 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=\overset{^}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, using the distance formula, the distance between $\mathbf{x}$ and the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}d(x,\overset{^}{x}) & =‖x-\overset{^}{x}‖ \\  & =\sqrt{({x}_{1}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{1})^{2}+({x}_{2}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{2})^{2}+({x}_{3}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{3})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(0-(-2))^{2}+(2-2)^{2}+(4-2)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+0+4} \\  & =\sqrt{8} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** Recall that the vector $\textbf{x}-\textrm{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x},$ whose norm $\| \textbf{x}-\textrm{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x} \|$ represents the distance from $\mathbf{x}$ to $S,$ is sometimes called the **vector rejection of $\mathbf{x}$ from $S.$**" :tutorial/id #uuid "97ecd7fd-ac4d-5cca-86c7-db064dd69609" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6131 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "290e4663-8f35-58a4-8aae-e48323b5562f" :step/math-academy-id 37246 :step/next {:db/id 17592186184942}} {:db/id 17592186184986 :step/content {:db/id 17592186184207 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186184111 :question/id #uuid "98aed663-0f72-5494-9a5f-ba2fdf94764a" :question/math-academy-id "e-9906"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "1224e2dd-96bc-5c24-aacf-3c36a7c3a1e1" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049045}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186184779} {:db/id 17592186184854} {:db/id 17592186269227} {:db/id 17592186269228} {:db/id 17592186269229} {:db/id 17592186269233} {:db/id 17592186269234} {:db/id 17592186326788} {:db/id 17592186354518} {:db/id 17592186369720}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Acute Angle Between a Vector and a Subspace"} :step/id #uuid "176d8f71-b7e6-5f7f-ace6-c9db9b253e57" :step/math-academy-id 37247 :step/next {:db/id 17592186184943}} {:db/id 17592186184987 :step/content {:db/id 17592186185334 :tutorial/content "As well as finding the distance between a vector and a subspace, we can also use the vector's orthogonal projection onto the subspace to find the angle between the vector and the subspace.

Given a vector $\mathbf{x}$ and a subspace $S = \textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \},$ the **acute angle between $\mathbf{x}$ and $S$** is the acute angle formed by $\mathbf{x}$ and its orthogonal projection $\textrm{proj}_S \mathbf{x},$ as shown below:

![](images/1c/1c9fd00ab46691fefc65ffa6478ed589fbad1df6bfd19b913c6a4a94ae0358a0.png)

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

We can compute the cosine of the angle between $\mathbf x$ and $\textrm{proj}_S \mathbf x$ using the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}\theta  & =\frac{x\cdot {\text{proj}}_{S}x}{||x||\cdot ||{\text{proj}}_{S}x||} \\  & =\frac{0\cdot (-2)+2\cdot 2+4\cdot 2}{\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{4}^{2}}\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{12}{\sqrt{20}\sqrt{12}} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 2\cdot 3}{2\sqrt{5}\cdot 2\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\theta = \arccos\left(  \dfrac{\sqrt3}{\sqrt5}\right) \approx 39.23^{\circ},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

[math]\qquad[/math] [math]\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 2 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} \quad[/math] and [math]\quad \dfrac12 \, \textrm{proj}_S \mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.[/math] 

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

\cos\theta 
&= \dfrac{0 \cdot (-1) + 2 \cdot 1 + 4 \cdot 1}{\sqrt{0^2+2^2+4^2}\sqrt{(-1)^2+1^2+1^2}} \\[5pt] 
&= \dfrac{6}{\sqrt{20}\sqrt3} \\[5pt] 
&= \dfrac{2\cdot3}{2\sqrt5\sqrt3} \\[5pt] 
&= \dfrac{\sqrt3}{\sqrt5}.  
\end{align}" :tutorial/id #uuid "4c19ec4b-3bdc-50e9-aac0-193e2ab2c298" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6132 :tutorial/title "Angle Between a Vector and a Subspace"} :step/id #uuid "53d452ce-ad18-557e-8201-0b1f1d4b9e5a" :step/math-academy-id 37248 :step/next {:db/id 17592186184986}}] :activity/title "Projecting Vectors Onto Subspaces in Euclidean Spaces (Arbitrary Bases): Applications" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186184403} {:db/id 17592186184985 :step/content {:db/id 17592186185333 :tutorial/content "One use for finding the orthogonal projection of a vector onto a subspace is to find the shortest distance between the vector and the subspace.

\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 4 & 9\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}9 & -4 \\ -4 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=\overset{^}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, using the distance formula, the distance between $\mathbf{x}$ and the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}d(x,\overset{^}{x}) & =‖x-\overset{^}{x}‖ \\  & =\sqrt{({x}_{1}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{1})^{2}+({x}_{2}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{2})^{2}+({x}_{3}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{3})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(0-(-2))^{2}+(2-2)^{2}+(4-2)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+0+4} \\  & =\sqrt{8} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** Recall that the vector $\textbf{x}-\textrm{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x},$ whose norm $\| \textbf{x}-\textrm{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x} \|$ represents the distance from $\mathbf{x}$ to $S,$ is sometimes called the **vector rejection of $\mathbf{x}$ from $S.$**" :tutorial/id #uuid "97ecd7fd-ac4d-5cca-86c7-db064dd69609" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6131 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186184986 :step/content {:db/id 17592186184207 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186184111 :question/id #uuid "98aed663-0f72-5494-9a5f-ba2fdf94764a" :question/math-academy-id "e-9906"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "1224e2dd-96bc-5c24-aacf-3c36a7c3a1e1" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049045}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186184779} {:db/id 17592186184854} {:db/id 17592186269227} {:db/id 17592186269228} {:db/id 17592186269229} {:db/id 17592186269233} {:db/id 17592186269234} {:db/id 17592186326788} {:db/id 17592186354518} {:db/id 17592186369720}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Acute Angle Between a Vector and a Subspace"} :step/id #uuid "176d8f71-b7e6-5f7f-ace6-c9db9b253e57" :step/math-academy-id 37247 :step/next {:db/id 17592186184943}} {:db/id 17592186185334 :tutorial/content "As well as finding the distance between a vector and a subspace, we can also use the vector's orthogonal projection onto the subspace to find the angle between the vector and the subspace.

Given a vector $\mathbf{x}$ and a subspace $S = \textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \},$ the **acute angle between $\mathbf{x}$ and $S$** is the acute angle formed by $\mathbf{x}$ and its orthogonal projection $\textrm{proj}_S \mathbf{x},$ as shown below:

![](images/1c/1c9fd00ab46691fefc65ffa6478ed589fbad1df6bfd19b913c6a4a94ae0358a0.png)

Let's return to our previous example, where we had

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Previously, we found that the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ into the subspace spanned by $\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}$ is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

We can compute the cosine of the angle between $\mathbf x$ and $\textrm{proj}_S \mathbf x$ using the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}\theta  & =\frac{x\cdot {\text{proj}}_{S}x}{||x||\cdot ||{\text{proj}}_{S}x||} \\  & =\frac{0\cdot (-2)+2\cdot 2+4\cdot 2}{\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{4}^{2}}\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{12}{\sqrt{20}\sqrt{12}} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 2\cdot 3}{2\sqrt{5}\cdot 2\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\theta = \arccos\left(  \dfrac{\sqrt3}{\sqrt5}\right) \approx 39.23^{\circ},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

Now, the acute angle between [math]\mathbf{x}[/math] and [math]\textrm{proj}_S \mathbf{x}[/math] is equivalent to the acute angle between [math]\mathbf{x}[/math] and any non-zero vector that is parallel to [math]\textrm{proj}_S \mathbf{x}.[/math] So, to make calculations easier, we can find the angle between the vectors

[math]\qquad[/math] [math]\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 2 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} \quad[/math] and [math]\quad \dfrac12 \, \textrm{proj}_S \mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.[/math] 

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

\begin{align}
\cos\theta 
&= \dfrac{0 \cdot (-1) + 2 \cdot 1 + 4 \cdot 1}{\sqrt{0^2+2^2+4^2}\sqrt{(-1)^2+1^2+1^2}} \\[5pt] 
&= \dfrac{6}{\sqrt{20}\sqrt3} \\[5pt] 
&= \dfrac{2\cdot3}{2\sqrt5\sqrt3} \\[5pt] 
&= \dfrac{\sqrt3}{\sqrt5}.  
\end{align}" :tutorial/id #uuid "4c19ec4b-3bdc-50e9-aac0-193e2ab2c298" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6132 :tutorial/title "Angle Between a Vector and a Subspace"} {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident
